$\begin{matrix} {\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial\left( \rho|\mathbf{u}|^{2} \right)}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}\left( \rho|\mathbf{u}|^{2} \right) \right)} & & \\ {= \rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\left( \left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( \rho\mathbf{u} \right) + 2\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u} \right) \right)} & & \\ {= \rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}\left( \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho\mathbf{u} \right) \right)} & & \\ {= -\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\sigma}} & & \\ & & {= -\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{\sigma} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) + \mathbf{\sigma}:\nabla\mathbf{u}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.181)

(3.181)

The internal energy balance equation can be then expressed as

$\frac{\partial\vartheta}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \vartheta\mathbf{u} \right) = \nabla \cdot \left( c\left( \nabla n \otimes \nabla n \right) \cdot \mathbf{u}-\left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}n \right) \right)c\nabla n \right)-\nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}-\mathbf{\sigma}:\nabla\mathbf{u}.$ (3.182)

(3.182)

We denote the bulk internal energy density by ϑb. Then the thermodynamical relation gives

ϑb = fb + sbT. (3.183)

(3.183)

Furthermore, we denote by ϑ∇ the gradient contribution of internal energy density, and from the thermodynamical relation and formulations of f∇ and s∇, we obtain

$\vartheta_{\nabla} = f_{\nabla} + s_{\nabla}T = \frac{1}{2}\left( c\left( T \right)-Tc^{\prime}\left( T \right) \right)\nabla n \cdot \nabla n.$ (3.184)

(3.184)

Theorem The gradients of pressure, temperature, and chemical potential have the following relation:

n∇μ + s∇T = ∇p + ∇ ⋅ c(∇n⊗∇n). (3.185)

(3.185)

Then the momentum balance equation can be reformulated into a conservation form

$\frac{\partial\left( \rho\mathbf{u} \right)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho\mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u} \right) = -n\nabla\mu-s\nabla T + \nabla \cdot \eta D\left( \mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla\left( \lambda\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right),$ (3.186)

(3.186)

or a convective form

$\rho\left( {\frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}} \right) = -n\nabla\mu-s\nabla T + \nabla \cdot \eta D\left( \mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla\left( \lambda\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right),$ (3.187)

(3.187)

which demonstrates that the gradients of chemical potential and temperature are the primal driving force.

The energy balance equation can be similarly modified as

$\begin{matrix} {\frac{\partial\vartheta}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \vartheta\mathbf{u} \right) = -\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{q}-c\left( \nabla n \otimes \nabla n \right) \cdot \mathbf{u} + \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}n \right) \right)c\nabla n \right)} \\ {-p\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}-\left( c\nabla n \otimes \nabla n \right):\nabla\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{\sigma}_{\text{irrev}}:\nabla\mathbf{u}} \\ {= -\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{u}p + \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}n \right) \right)c\nabla n \right)} \\ {+ \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla p + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \left( c\nabla n \otimes \nabla n \right)-\mathbf{\sigma}_{\text{irrev}}:\nabla\mathbf{u}} \\ {= -\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{u}p + \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}n \right) \right)c\nabla n \right)} \\ {+ \mathbf{u} \cdot \left( n\nabla\mu + s\nabla T \right)-\mathbf{\sigma}_{\text{irrev}}:\nabla\mathbf{u}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.188)

(3.188)

Moving the term ∇ ⋅ (uf) into the left-hand side and taking into account ϑ = f + Ts, we obtain the balance equation of internal energy density

$\begin{matrix} {\frac{\partial\vartheta}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}\left( n\mu + \mathit{sT} \right) = -\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{q} + \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}n \right) \right)c\nabla n \right)} \\ {+ \mathbf{u} \cdot \left( n\nabla\mu + s\nabla T \right)-\mathbf{\sigma}_{\text{irrev}}:\nabla\mathbf{u}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.189)

(3.189)

3.3.2 Thermodynamical consistent algorithm

The bulk Helmholtz free energy density fb can be split into two parts: one is a convex function with respect to n, denoted by fbconvex(n,T), and the other is a concave function with respect to n, denoted by fbconcave(n,T), which are formulated as

fbconvex(n,T) = fbideal(n,T) + fbrepulsion(n,T), (3.190)

(3.190)

fbconcave(n,T) = fbattraction(n,T). (3.191)

(3.191)

The gradient contribution to the Helmholtz free energy density is always convex with respect to molar density. Moreover, it is concave with respect to the temperature if we take the temperature such that

$\left( 1 + m \right)\left( \beta_{1}\left( 1-T_{r} \right) + \beta_{2} \right) + 4\beta_{1}T_{r}\left( 1 + m\left( 1-\sqrt{T_{r}} \right) \right) \leq 0,$ (3.192)

(3.192)

where Tr = T/Tc. In the previous equation, it should be noted that the parameter has a negative value, while the rest parameters are positive, so the satisfaction of Eq. (3.192) is reasonable. We have checked in numerical tests that the previous condition is satisfied for butane when the temperature lies in a large range from 0.1 Tc to 3 Tc, where Tc is the critical temperature of butane.

A semiimplicit time marching scheme accounting for the convex-splitting of Helmholtz free energy density is used to discretize the chemical potential:

μk + 1 = μbk + 1 + μ∇(nk + 1,Tk + 1), μbk + 1 = μbconvex(nk + 1,Tk + 1) + μbconcave(nk,Tk + 1). (3.193)

(3.193)

We define an auxiliary velocity as

$\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} = \mathbf{u}^{k}-\frac{\delta t_{k}}{\rho^{k}}\left( n^{k}\nabla\mu^{k + 1} + s^{k}\nabla T^{k + 1} \right),$ (3.194)

(3.194)

where ρk = nkMw. On the boundary, we take nk∇μk + 1 + sk∇Tk + 1 = 0 for u*k, and as a result, we have still u*k = 0 on the boundary. u*k can be viewed as an approximation of uk + 1 obtained by neglecting the convection and viscosity terms in the momentum balance equation. Subsequently, a semiimplicit scheme is designed as

$\frac{n^{k + 1}-n^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + \nabla \cdot \left( n^{k}{\mathbf{u}_{*}}^{k} \right) = 0,$ (3.195)

(3.195)

$\begin{matrix} & & {\frac{\rho^{k + 1}\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \otimes \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right) = -n^{k}\nabla\mu^{k + 1}-s^{k}\nabla T^{k + 1}} \\ & & {+ \nabla \cdot \eta^{k}D\left( \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right) + \nabla\left( \lambda^{k}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.196)

(3.196)

$\begin{matrix} {\frac{\vartheta^{k + 1}-\vartheta^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}\left( n^{k}\mu^{k + 1} + s^{k}T^{k + 1} \right) = -\nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}^{k + 1}} \\ {-\nabla \cdot \left( \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}n^{k} \right) \right)c^{k + 1}\nabla n^{k + 1} \right) + \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \cdot \left( n^{k}\nabla\mu^{k + 1} + s^{k}\nabla T^{k + 1} \right)} \\ {+ \eta^{k}D\left( \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right):\nabla\mathbf{u}^{k + 1} + \lambda^{k}|\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{k + 1}|^{2}} \\ {+ \frac{\rho^{k}}{2\delta t_{k}}\left( |\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-{\mathbf{u}_{*}}^{k}|^{2} + |\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}-\mathbf{u}^{k}|^{2} \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.197)

(3.197)

where qk + 1 =  − Θk∇Tk + 1, Θk = Θ(nk,Tk).

Using Eq. (4.142), it can be further derived that

$\begin{matrix} {\rho^{k + 1}\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} + \delta t_{k}\nabla \cdot \left( \rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \otimes \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right)} \\ {= \rho^{k + 1}\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} + \delta t_{k}\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}\nabla \cdot \left( \rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \right) + \delta t_{k}\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}} \\ {= \rho^{k + 1}\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}-\left( \rho^{k + 1}-\rho^{k} \right)\mathbf{u}^{k + 1} + \delta t_{k}\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}} \\ {= \rho^{k}\left( \mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \right) + \delta t_{k}\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}^{k + 1},} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.198)

(3.198)

which allows us to reformulate Eq. (4.143) as

$\rho^{k}\frac{\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + \rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}^{k + 1} = \nabla \cdot \eta^{k}D\left( \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right) + \nabla\left( \lambda^{k}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right).$ (3.199)

(3.199)

Similarly, Eq. (4.144) can be reformulated as

$\begin{matrix} {\frac{\vartheta^{k + 1}-\vartheta^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + T^{k + 1}\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}s^{k} \right) = -\nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}^{k + 1}} \\ {-\nabla \cdot \left( \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}n^{k} \right) \right)c^{k + 1}\nabla n^{k + 1} \right)-\mu^{k + 1}\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}n^{k} \right)} \\ {+ \eta^{k}D\left( \mathbf{u}^{k + 1} \right):\nabla\mathbf{u}^{k + 1} + \lambda^{k}|\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{k + 1}|^{2}} \\ {+ \frac{\rho^{k}}{2\delta t_{k}}\left( |\mathbf{u}^{k + 1}-{\mathbf{u}_{*}}^{k}|^{2} + |\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}-\mathbf{u}^{k}|^{2} \right).} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.200)

(3.200)

The algorithm is thermodynamically consistent as the discrete Helmholtz free energy densities satisfy

$\begin{matrix} \frac{f^{k + 1}-f^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} & {\leq -s^{k}\frac{T^{k + 1}-T^{k}}{\delta t_{k}}-\mu^{k + 1}\nabla \cdot \left( n^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k} \right)} \\ {-\nabla \cdot \left( \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k}n^{k} \right) \right)c^{k + 1}\nabla n^{k + 1} \right),} & \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.201)

(3.201)

where fk = f(nk,Tk). To solve the discrete systems efficiently, with the help of the auxiliary velocity, we propose the following fully decoupled, linearized iterative method:

$\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l} = \mathbf{u}^{k}-\frac{\delta t_{k}}{\rho^{k}}\left( n^{k}\nabla\mu^{k + 1,l + 1} + s^{k}\nabla T^{k + 1,l} \right),$ (3.202)

(3.202)

$\frac{n^{k + 1,l + 1}-n^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + \nabla \cdot \left( n^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l} \right) = 0,$ (3.203)

(3.203)

$\begin{matrix} {\frac{\rho^{k + 1,l + 1}\mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1}-\rho^{k}\mathbf{u}^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho^{k}\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l} \otimes \mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1} \right) = -n^{k}\nabla\mu^{k + 1,l + 1}-s^{k}\nabla T^{k,l}} \\ {+ \nabla \cdot \eta^{k}D\left( \mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1} \right) + \nabla\left( \lambda^{k}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1} \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.204)

(3.204)

$\begin{matrix} {\frac{\vartheta^{k + 1,l + 1}-\vartheta^{k}}{\delta t_{k}} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l}\left( n^{k}\mu^{k + 1,l + 1} + s^{k}T^{k + 1,l} \right)} \\ {= \nabla \cdot \Theta^{k}\nabla T^{k + 1,l + 1}-\nabla \cdot \left( \left( \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l}n^{k} \right) \right)c^{k + 1,l}\nabla n^{k + 1,l + 1} \right)} \\ {+ \mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l} \cdot \left( n^{k}\nabla\mu^{k + 1,l + 1} + s^{k}\nabla T^{k + 1,l} \right) + \eta^{k}D\left( \mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1} \right):\nabla\mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1}} \\ {+ \lambda^{k}|\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1}|^{2} + \frac{1}{2\delta t_{k}}\rho^{k}\left( |\mathbf{u}^{k + 1,l + 1}-\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l}|^{2} + |\mathbf{u}_{*}^{k,l}-\mathbf{u}^{k}|^{2} \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.205)

(3.205)

where the superscripts l and l + 1 denote the lth and (l+1)th iterations, respectively, and μk + 1, l + 1, ϑk + 1, l + 1 are defined as

$\begin{matrix} {\mu^{k + 1,l + 1} = \mu_{b}^{\text{convex}}\left( n^{k + 1,l},T^{k + 1,l} \right) + \frac{\partial\mu_{b}^{\text{convex}}}{\partial n}\left( n^{k + 1,l},T^{k + 1,l} \right)\left( n^{k + 1,l + 1}-n^{k + 1,l} \right)} \\ {+ \mu_{b}^{\text{concave}}\left( n^{k},T^{k + 1,l} \right) + \mu_{\nabla}\left( n^{k + 1,l + 1},T^{k + 1,l} \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$ (3.206)

(3.206)

$\vartheta^{k + 1,l + 1} = \vartheta\left( n^{k + 1,l + 1},T^{k + 1,l} \right) + \frac{\partial\vartheta}{\partial T}\left( n^{k + 1,l + 1},T^{k + 1,l} \right)\left( T^{k + 1,l + 1}-T^{k + 1,l} \right).$ (3.207)

(3.207)

3.3.3 Scalar auxiliary variable scheme

It is needed a thorough consideration that the energy dissipation mechanism should be kept automatically in the process, when constructing the scheme. Otherwise, it may require a time step extremely small to keep the energy dissipation. For a general free energy functional contains a quadratic term, to obtain an energy dissipative scheme, the linear term is usually treated implicitly in some manners, while different approaches have to be used for nonlinear terms (

We first write the Helmholtz free energy as the following form:

$F = \int_{\Omega}\left\lbrack {\frac{C}{2}|\nabla n|^{2} + f} \right\rbrack\mathit{dx},$ (3.208)

(3.208)

for a fourth-order two-phase model as nt + cΔ2n = Δμ0.C is the influence parameter. The homogeneous term of the free energy has the following form:

Ep∫Ωfdx. (3.209)

(3.209)

The main idea of the SAV scheme is to introduce the following term:

$r(t) = \sqrt{E_{p} + C_{0}},$ (3.210)

(3.210)

where C0 is a constant to ensure that Ep + C0 ≥ 0. Therefore the total Helmholtz free energy will be rewritten as

$F = \int_{\Omega}\left. \frac{C}{2} \middle| \nabla n|^{2} \right.dx + r^{2} - C_{0}.$ (3.211)

(3.211)

The fluid can be then modeled by the following numerical scheme:

$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {n_{t} = \Delta\mu;} \\ {\mu = - C\Delta n + \frac{r}{\sqrt{E_{p} + C_{0}}}\mu_{0}(n);} \\ {r_{t} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{E_{p} + C_{0}}}\int_{\Omega}{\mu_{0}(n)n_{t}}dx,} \\ \end{array} \right.$ (3.212)

(3.212)

where μ0 = ∂f0/∂n and this system can be generalized into

$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {n_{t} + C\Delta^{2}n - \frac{r}{\sqrt{E_{p} + C_{0}}}\Delta\mu_{0}} \\ {r_{t} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{E_{p} + C_{0}}}\int_{\Omega}{\mu_{0}(n)n_{t}}dx.} \\ \end{array} \right.$ (3.213)

(3.213)

Numerical discretization to the previous system can lead to

$\frac{n^{k + 1} - n^{k}}{\Delta t} + C\Delta_{h}^{2}n^{k + 1} - \frac{r^{k + 1}}{\sqrt{E_{p}(k^{n}) + C_{0}}}\Delta_{h}\mu_{0}(n^{k}) = 0$ (3.214)

(3.214)

$r^{k + 1} - r^{k} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{E_{p}(n^{k}) + C_{0}}}\int_{\Omega}{\mu_{0}(n^{n})(n^{k + 1} - n^{k})}dx$ (3.215)

(3.215)

Solving nk + 1 from Eq. (3.214) can lead to

$n^{k + 1} = {(1 + \Delta tC\Delta_{h}^{2})}^{- 1}n^{k} + dt\frac{r^{k + 1}}{\sqrt{E_{p}(n^{k}) + C_{0}}}{(1 + \Delta tC\Delta_{h}^{2})}^{- 1}\Delta_{h}\mu_{0}(n^{k}).$ (3.216)

(3.216)

Substituting this evolution formula back into Eq. (3.215), the calculation of rk + 1 can be expressed as

$r^{k + 1} = \frac{r^{k} + \left( {1/\left( {2\sqrt{E_{p}(n^{k}) + C_{0}}} \right)} \right)\int_{\Omega}{\mu_{0}(n^{k})\left\lbrack {(1 + \Delta tC\Delta_{h}^{2})}^{- 1} - 1 \right\rbrack n^{k}}dx}{1 - \left( {{\Delta t}/\left( {2(E_{p}(n^{k}) + C_{0})} \right)} \right)\int{\mu_{0}(n^{k}){(1 + \Delta tC\Delta_{h}^{2})}^{- 1}\Delta_{h}\mu_{0}(n^{k})dx}}.$ (3.217)

(3.217)

Advantage of this scheme lies on the fact that we only solve the linear system at each time step and the coefficient is fixed at each time step. This is very different from the IEQ scheme that has the variable coefficient. Constant coefficient makes it possible for us to use the fast Fourier transformation to solve the linear system. This will greatly reduce the time spent in the calculation.

This algorithm is unconditionally energy stable, which can be simply proved as (

$\begin{array}{l} {(\Delta_{h}\mu^{k + 1},\mu^{k + 1})} \\ {= \left( {- C\Delta_{h}n^{k + 1},\frac{n^{k + 1} - n^{k}}{\Delta t}} \right) + 2r^{k + 1}\frac{r^{k + 1} - r^{k}}{\Delta t}} \\ {= \frac{1}{2\Delta t}\left\lbrack ( - C\Delta_{h}n^{k + 1},n^{k + 1}) - ( - C\Delta_{h}n^{k},n^{k}) + ( - C\Delta_{h}(n^{k + 1} - n^{k}),n^{k + 1} - n^{k}) \right\rbrack + \frac{1}{\Delta t}({(r^{k + 1})}^{2} - {(r^{k})}^{2} + {(r^{k + 1} - r^{k})}^{2})} \\ {= \frac{1}{\Delta t}({\widehat{F}}^{k + 1} - {\widehat{F}}^{k}) + \frac{1}{2\Delta t}\left\lbrack ( - C\Delta_{h}(n^{k + 1} - n^{k}),n^{k + 1} - n^{k}) + 2{(r^{k + 1} - r^{k})}^{2} \right\rbrack} \\ \end{array}$ (3.218)

(3.218)

Note that F̂k has the form F̂ = (1/2)(n,  − CΔn) + r2 and Δh is a nonpositive symmetric operator, so that it is easy to get

F̂k + 1 − F̂k ≤ 0. (3.219)

(3.219)

The mass conservation property of our scheme can also be quickly proved as

$\int_{\Omega}\frac{n^{k + 1} - n^{k}}{\Delta_{t}}dx = \int_{\Omega} - C\Delta^{2}n + \frac{r}{\sqrt{E_{p} + C_{0}}}\Delta\mu_{0}(n)dx,$ (3.220)

(3.220)

and for periodic boundary condition, we can find that the right-hand side of the previous equation equals to zero. Thus we can have

∫Ωnk + 1dx = ∫Ωnkdx. (3.221)

(3.221)

A second-order SAV can also be constructed. Using the Crank–Nicolson scheme on the time and it can lead to

$\frac{n^{k + 1} - n^{k}}{\Delta t} + \frac{C}{2}\Delta_{h}^{2}(n^{k + 1} + n^{k}) - \frac{r^{k + 1} + r^{k}}{2\sqrt{E_{p}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)}) + C_{0}}}\Delta_{h}\mu_{0}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)}) = 0$ (3.222)

(3.222)

$r^{k + 1} - r^{k} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{E_{p}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)}) + C_{0}}}\int_{\Omega}{\mu_{0}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})(n^{k + 1} - n^{k})}dx$ (3.223)

(3.223)

where the n̂k + (1/2) can be regarded as any explicit approximation of the nk + (1/2). However, due to the high nonlinearity of PR-EOS, it works not very well with an explicit approximation here. So need a semiexplicit scheme as

$\frac{{\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)} - n^{k}}{\Delta t/2} = - C\Delta_{h}^{2}{\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)} + \Delta\mu_{0}(n^{k}).$ (3.224)

(3.224)

Then, the update of nk + 1 can lead to

$n^{k + 1} = \left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\Delta tC\Delta_{h}^{2}} \right)^{- 1}\left( {1 - \frac{1}{2}dtC\Delta_{h}^{2}} \right)n^{k} + \Delta_{t}\frac{r^{k + 1} + r^{k}}{2\sqrt{E_{p}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)}) + C_{0}}}{(1 + \Delta tC\Delta_{h}^{2})}^{- 1}\Delta_{h}\mu_{0}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)}).$ (3.225)

(3.225)

Finally, the rk + 1 term can be calculated as

$\begin{array}{l} {r^{k + 1} = \left( {r^{k} + \int_{\Omega}\frac{\mu_{0}(n^{k + (1/2)})}{2\sqrt{E_{p}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})}}\left\lbrack {\left( {1 + \Delta t\frac{1}{2}C\Delta_{h}^{2}} \right)^{- 1}\left( {1 - \Delta t\frac{1}{2}C\Delta_{h}^{2}} \right) - 1} \right\rbrack n^{k}\Delta t} \right.} \\ \left. {+ \int_{\Omega}\Delta t\frac{r^{k}\mu_{0}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})}{4E_{p}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})}\left( {1 + \Delta t\frac{1}{2}C\Delta_{h}^{2}} \right)^{- 1}\Delta_{h}\mu_{0}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})dx} \right) \\ {{/\left( {1 - \int_{\Omega}\Delta t\frac{\mu_{0}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})}{4E_{p}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})}\left( {1 + \Delta t\frac{1}{2}C\Delta_{h}^{2}} \right)^{- 1}\Delta_{h}\mu_{0}({\widehat{n}}^{k + (1/2)})dx} \right)}.} \\ \end{array}$ (3.226)

(3.226)

The unconditional energy stability can be similarly proved as well as the mass conservation. Furthermore, like the first-order scheme, we only solve the linear system at each time step and the coefficients are still fixed at each time step.

3.4 Multiphase flow with partial miscibility

For realistic fluids the diffuse interfaces always exist between two phases. The interfacial partial miscibility is a phenomenon that the two-phase fluids behave on the interfaces. To model this feature a local density gradient contribution is introduced into the Helmholtz free energy density of inhomogeneous fluids. The general form of Helmholtz free energy density (denoted by f) is then the sum of two contributions: Helmholtz free energy density of bulk homogeneous fluid and a local density gradient contribution f = fb + f∇, where $f_{\nabla} = \left( 1/2 \right)\sum_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}.$ Here, cij is the cross influence parameter with symmetry cij = cji. The density gradient contribution accounts for the phase transition by the gradual density changes of each component on the interfaces.

3.4.1 Thermodynamic preparations

Recall the first law of thermodynamics

$\frac{d\left( U + E \right)}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{\mathit{dW}}{\mathit{dt}} + \frac{\mathit{dQ}}{\mathit{dt}},$ (3.227)

(3.227)

where t is the time, U is the internal energy, E is the kinetic energy, W is the work done by the face force Ft, and Q stands for the heat transfer from the surrounding that occurs to keep the system temperature constant. We split the total entropy S into a summation of two contributions. One is the entropy of the system, denoted by Ssys. The other is the entropy of the surrounding, denoted by Ssurr, that has the relation with Q as $dS_{\text{surr}} = -\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{T}.$ Taking into account the relation U = F + TSsys, we can get

$\frac{\mathit{dS}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{dS_{\text{sys}}}{\mathit{dt}} + \frac{dS_{\text{surr}}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{dS_{\text{sys}}}{\mathit{dt}}-\frac{1}{T}\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{dS_{\text{sys}}}{\mathit{dt}}-\frac{1}{T}\left( {\frac{d\left( U + E \right)}{\mathit{dt}}-\frac{\mathit{dW}}{\mathit{dt}}} \right) = -\frac{1}{T}\frac{d\left( F + E \right)}{\mathit{dt}} + \frac{1}{T}\frac{\mathit{dW}}{\mathit{dt}}.$ (3.228)

(3.228)

We denote by Mw, i the molar weight of component i and define the mass density of the mixture as $\rho = \sum_{i = 1}^{M}n_{i}M_{w,i}.$ In a time-dependent volume V(t), we define the entropy, Helmholtz free energy, and kinetic energy within V(t) as

$S = \int_{V(t)}s\mathit{dV},F = \int_{V(t)}\mathit{fdV},E = \frac{1}{2}\int_{V(t)}{\rho{|\mathbf{u}|}^{2}\mathit{dV}},$ (3.229)

(3.229)

where s is the entropy density and u is a specified or average velocity of the mixture, such as the mass-average velocity and molar-average velocity. Applying the Reynolds transport theorem and the Gauss divergence theorem, we deduce that

$\frac{\mathit{dS}}{\mathit{dt}} = \int_{V(t)}{\frac{\partial s}{\partial t}\mathit{dV}} + \int_{V(t)}{\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}s} \right)\mathit{dV}},$ (3.230)

(3.230)

$\frac{\mathit{dF}}{\mathit{dt}} = \int_{V(t)}{\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\mathit{dV}} + \int_{V(t)}{\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}f} \right)\mathit{dV}},$ (3.231)

(3.231)

and

$\frac{\mathit{dE}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_{V(t)}{\frac{\partial\left( {\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)}{\partial t}\mathit{dV}} + \frac{1}{2}\int_{V(t)}{\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}\left( {\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)} \right)\mathit{dV}} = \int_{V(t)}{\left( {\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}} \right)\mathit{dV}} + \frac{1}{2}\int_{V(t)}\left( \left( {\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} + \left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\rho + \rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right) \right)\mathit{dV} = \int_{V(t)}{\left( {\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}} \right)\mathit{dV}} + \frac{1}{2}\int_{V(t)}\left( \left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {\rho\mathbf{u}} \right) + 2\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}} \right) \right)\mathit{dV} = \int_{V(t)}{\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( {\frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}} \right)\mathit{dV}} + \frac{1}{2}\int_{V(t)}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}\left( {\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\rho\mathbf{u}} \right)} \right)\mathit{dV}}.$ (3.232)

(3.232)

In the presence of a fluid velocity field, the mass transfer in fluids takes place through the convection in addition to the diffusion of each component. Thus the mass balance law for component i gives us

$\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{i}} \right) + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i} = 0,$ (3.233)

(3.233)

where Ji is the diffusion flux of component i. Multiplying Eq. (3.233) by Mw, i and summing them from i = 1 to M, we obtain the mass balance equation

$\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho\mathbf{u} \right) + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}M_{w,i}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i} = 0.$ (3.234)

(3.234)

We note that the diffusion term in the previous equation vanishes if u is the mass-average velocity, but it may still exist for the other average velocity, for example, molar-average velocity frequently employed in multicomponent fluids. Substituting Eq. (3.234) into Eq. (3.232), we can get

$\frac{\mathit{dE}}{\mathit{dt}} = \int_{V(t)}{\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \frac{d\mathbf{u}}{\mathit{dt}}\mathit{dV}}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{V{(t)}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)\left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathit{dV}}} = \int_{V{(t)}}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( {\rho\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{\mathit{dt}} + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}}} \right)\mathit{dV}}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{V{(t)}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)\mathit{dV}}},$ (3.235)

(3.235)

where (du/dt) = (∂u/∂t) + u ⋅ ∇u. The work done by Ft is expressed as (dW/dt) = ∫∂V(t)Ft ⋅ uds.

Cauchy’s relation between face force Ft and the stress tensor σ of component i gives Ft =  − σ ⋅ ν, and as a result,

$\frac{\mathit{dW}}{\mathit{dt}} = -\int_{\partial V(t)}\left( {\mathbf{\sigma} \cdot \mathbf{\nu}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{u}d\mathbf{s} = -\int_{V(t)}{\left( {\mathbf{\sigma}^{T}:\nabla\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\sigma} \right)} \right)\mathit{dV}},$ (3.236)

(3.236)

where ν is the unit normal vector toward the outside of V(t). We note that the other external forces, including gravity force, are ignored in this work, but the model derivations can be easily extended to the cases in the presence of external forces.

The entropy balance equation can be constructed on the basis of the previous:

$T\left( {\frac{\partial s}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}s \right)} \right) = \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right)\mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}-\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}f} \right)-\mathbf{\sigma}^{T}:\nabla\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( {\rho\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{\mathit{dt}} + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\sigma}}} \right).$ (3.237)

(3.237)

From the definition of pb, we have

$\nabla p_{b} = \nabla\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{n_{i}\mu_{i}^{b}-f_{b}}} \right) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i}^{b} + \mu_{i}^{b}\nabla n_{i}-\mu_{i}^{b}\nabla n_{i}} \right) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i}^{b}.$ (3.238)

(3.238)

Combing the previous equation together with the mass balance Eq. (3.233), the transport equation of Helmholtz free energy density fb can be calculated as

$\frac{\partial f_{b}}{\partial t} = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}^{b}\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t} = -\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}^{b}\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( n_{i}\mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i}} \right) = -\nabla \cdot \left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}n_{i}\mu_{i}^{b}\mathbf{u}-p_{b}\mathbf{u}} \right)-\nabla \cdot \left( p_{b}\mathbf{u} \right) + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}n_{i}\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mu_{i}^{b}-\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}^{b}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i} = -\nabla \cdot \left( f_{b}\mathbf{u} \right)-\nabla \cdot \left( p_{b}\mathbf{u} \right) + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla p_{b}-\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}^{b}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i} = -\nabla \cdot \left( f_{b}\mathbf{u} \right)-p_{b}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}-\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}^{b}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i}.$ (3.239)

(3.239)

The gradient contribution of Helmholtz free energy density can be formulated as

$\frac{\partial f_{\nabla}}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial\left( {\sum_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right)}{\partial t} = \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla\frac{\partial n_{j}}{\partial t} = -\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{j}} \right) + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)$

$= -\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{j}} \right)} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}n_{j}\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right)},$ (3.240)

(3.240)

and

$\nabla \cdot \left( f_{\nabla}\mathbf{u} \right) = \frac{1}{2}\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{ij}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right) = \frac{1}{2}\left( {\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\left( {\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}}} \right).$ (3.241)

(3.241)

Combining the equations for all the contributions, the transport equation of the Helmholtz free energy can be deduced as

$\begin{array}{l} {{\frac{\partial\mathit{f}}{\partial\mathit{t}} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\mathit{f}\mathbf{u}} \right)}{= \frac{\partial\mathit{f}_{\mathit{b}}}{\partial\mathit{t}} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\mathit{f}_{\mathit{b}}\mathbf{u}} \right) + \frac{\partial\mathit{f}_{\nabla}}{\partial\mathit{t}} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\mathit{f}_{\nabla}\mathbf{u}} \right)}} \\ {= - \mathit{p}_{\mathit{b}}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} - \sum\limits_{\mathit{i} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\mathit{\mu}_{i}^{b}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{\mathit{i}} - \sum\limits_{\mathit{i},\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}\mathit{n}_{\mathit{j}}} \right)} \right)\mathit{c}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{i}}} \right)} \\ {+ \sum\limits_{\mathit{i},\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathit{n}_{\mathit{i}}\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathit{c}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{j}}} \right) + \sum\limits_{\mathit{i},\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{j}}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathit{c}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{i}}} \right)} \\ {- \sum\limits_{\mathit{i},\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot J_{\mathit{j}}} \right)\mathit{c}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{i}}} \right) + \sum\limits_{\mathit{i},\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{\mathit{j}}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathit{c}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{i}}} \right)} \\ {+ \frac{1}{2}\left( {\sum\limits_{\mathit{i},\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\mathit{c}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{i}} \cdot \nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{j}}} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u} \cdot \sum\limits_{\mathit{i},\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\nabla\left( {\mathit{c}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{i}} \cdot \nabla\mathit{n}_{\mathit{j}}} \right)} \\ {= - \left( {p_{b} - \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}n_{i}\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{ij}\nabla n_{j}} \right) - \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{ij}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}^{b}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i}} \\ {- \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{j}} \right)} \right)c_{ij}\nabla n_{i}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{ij}\nabla n_{i}} \right)} \\ {{- \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)c_{ij}\nabla n_{i}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{ij}\nabla n_{j}} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}}{\cdot \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla\left( {c_{ij}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right)}} \\ {= - p\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i} + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla n_{i}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{ij}\nabla n_{j}} \right) - \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla} \\ {{\cdot \left( {\left. \left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{j}} \right)} \right)c_{ij}\nabla n_{i} \right) - \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( \left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)c_{ij}\nabla n_{i} \right.} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}}{\cdot \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla\left( {c_{ij}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right).}} \\ \end{array}$ (3.242)

(3.242)

Taking the following identity into account

$\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\left( {\nabla n_{i}} \right)\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{j}} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla\left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \cdot \nabla n_{j}} \right) = \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right),$ (3.243)

(3.243)

we can reformulate the Helmholtz free energy transportation equation as

$\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( f\mathbf{u} \right) = -p\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}-\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mu_{i}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \left( {\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot c_{\mathit{ij}}\left( {\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)} \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{j}} \right)} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right) = -p\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{\mathit{ij}}\left( {\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)} \right)-\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\mu_{i}\mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( \left( \left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{j}} \right)} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \right. \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right)-\left( {\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}c_{\mathit{ij}}\left( {\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)} \right):\nabla\mathbf{u} + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mu_{i}.$ (3.244)

(3.244)

3.4.2 Model for realistic fluid flow

Substituting Eq. (3.244) back into Eq. (3.237), the entropy equation can be reformulated as

$T\left( {\frac{\partial s}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u}s \right)} \right) = \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right)\mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)}-\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u} \cdot \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{c_{\mathit{ij}}\left( {\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{\nabla \cdot \left( {\mu_{i}\mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)} + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{j}} \right)} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right)} + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{\nabla \cdot \left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{j}} \right)c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i}} \right)}-\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mu_{i}-\mathbf{\sigma}^{T}}:\nabla\mathbf{u} + \left( {p\mathbf{I} + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{c_{\mathit{ij}}\left( {\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)}} \right):\nabla\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( {\rho\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{\mathit{dt}} + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\sigma}}} \right),$ (3.245)

(3.245)

where I is the second-order identity tensor. Integrating the previous equation over the entire domain, we obtain the change of total entropy S with time

$T\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = -\int_{\Omega}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mu_{i}d\mathbf{x}}}-\int_{\Omega}\left( {\mathbf{\sigma}^{T}-p\mathbf{I}-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{c_{\mathit{ij}}\left( {\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)}} \right):\nabla\mathbf{u}d\mathbf{x}-\int_{\Omega}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \left( {\rho\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{\mathit{dt}} + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\sigma}}} \right)d\mathbf{x}},$ (3.246)

(3.246)

According to the second law of thermodynamics, the total entropy shall not decrease with time. Using this principle, we can determine the complete forms of multicomponent two-phase flow model. First, we consider an ideal reversible process to get the form of the reversible stress, and the reversibility implies that there exist no effects of viscosity and friction. In this case the entropy shall be conserved, so the diffusions vanish, that is, Ji = 0, and the total tress σ becomes equal to the reversible stress, denoted by σrev, which must have the form

$\mathbf{\sigma}_{\text{rev}} = p\mathbf{I} + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{c_{ij}\left( {\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)}.$ (3.247)

(3.247)

The last term on the right-hand side of Eq. (3.246) shall also be zero as

$\rho\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{\mathit{dt}} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\sigma}_{\text{rev}} = 0.$ (3.248)

(3.248)

For the realistic irreversible multicomponent chemical systems, the driving force for diffusion of each component is the gradient of chemical potentials, so we express the diffusion flux for each component as

$\mathbf{J}_{i} = -\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}{\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mu_{j}}, i = 1,\ldots,M,$ (3.249)

(3.249)

where ℳ = (ℳij)i, j = 1M is the mobility. Consequently, the mole balance equation for component i is stated as

$\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u}n_{i}} \right)-\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}{\nabla \cdot \mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mu_{j}} = 0,$ (3.250)

(3.250)

where i = 1, …, M. The mobility matrix ℳ shall be symmetric in terms of Onsager’s reciprocal principle. The second law of thermodynamics requires

$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mu_{i} \leq 0},$ (3.251)

(3.251)

which ensures the nonnegativity of the first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (3.246). A few choices of the mobility are provided to help readers select for different cases. In the following mobility formulations, R stands for the universal gas constant.

Mobility 1 We take ℳ as a diagonal positive definite matrix with diagonal elements ℳii = Dini/RT, and then we have the following diffusion flux Ji =  − (Dini/RT)∇μi, wehre Di > 0 is the diffusion coefficient of component. This mobility choice apparently satisfies Onsager’s reciprocal principle and the condition stated in Eq. (3.251). At constant temperature and pressure, it holds that $\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i}} = 0$ due to the Gibbs–Duhem equation, and furthermore, if taking D1 = ⋯ = DM, we derive $\sum_{i = 1}^{M}\mathbf{J}_{i} = 0$ at constant temperature and pressure.

Mobility 2 We take the mobility using molar-average velocity as

$\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ii}} = \sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{ij}}n_{i}n_{j}}{\mathit{nRT}},\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}} = -\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{ij}}n_{i}n_{j}}{\mathit{nRT}}, j \neq i,$ (3.252)

(3.252)

where $n = \sum_{j = 1}^{M}n_{j}$ and the mole diffusion coefficients 𝒟ij satisfy 𝒟ii = 0 and 𝒟ij = 𝒟ji > 0 for i ≠ j. This means that $\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ii}} = -\sum_{j = 1,j \neq i}^{M}\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}}$, so we have $\sum_{j = 1}^{M}\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}} = 0$ for any 1 ≤ i ≤ M and thus $\sum_{i = 1}^{M}\mathbf{J}_{i} = -\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{\sum_{j = 1}^{M}\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}}}\nabla\mu_{j} = -\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{\nabla\mu_{i}}\sum_{j = 1}^{M}\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}} = 0.$ This mobility is symmetric and thus it satisfies Onsager’s reciprocal principle.

Mobility 3 We denote ρi = niMw, i and take the mobility for mass-average velocity as

$\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ii}} = \sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{ij}}n_{i}\rho_{j}}{M_{w,i}\rho\mathit{RT}},\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}} = -\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{ij}}n_{i}n_{j}}{\rho\mathit{RT}}, j \neq i,$ (3.253)

(3.253)

where the mass diffusion coefficients 𝒟ij satisfy 𝒟ii = 0 and 𝒟ij = 𝒟ji > 0 for i ≠ j. It is obvious that this mobility is symmetric and Onsager’s reciprocal principle is satisfied. We further denote $\overline{\mathcal{M}} = \left( {\overline{\mathcal{M}}}_{\mathit{ij}} \right)_{i,j = 1}^{M}$ as ${\overline{\mathcal{M}}}_{\mathit{ii}} = M_{w,i}^{2}\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ii}} = \sum_{j = 1}^{M}\left( \mathcal{D}_{\mathit{ij}}\rho_{i}\rho_{j}/\rho\mathit{RT} \right),{\overline{\mathcal{M}}}_{\mathit{ij}} = M_{w,i}M_{w,j}\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}} = -\left( \mathcal{D}_{\mathit{ij}}\rho_{i}\rho_{j}/\rho\mathit{RT} \right),j \neq i.$ Apparently, $\overline{\mathcal{M}}$ is symmetric and it satisfies $\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{{\overline{\mathcal{M}}}_{\mathit{ij}} = 0}$ for any 1 ≤ j ≤ M, so we obtain $\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i}} = -\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{\sum_{j = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mu_{j}}} = -\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{\sum_{j = 1}^{M}{{\overline{\mathcal{M}}}_{\mathit{ij}}\left( \nabla\mu_{j}/M_{w,j} \right)}} = -\sum_{j = 1}^{M}\left( \nabla\mu_{j}/M_{w,j} \right)\sum_{i = 1}^{M}{{\overline{\mathcal{M}}}_{\mathit{ij}} = 0}.$

For the realistic viscous flow the total stress can be split into two parts: reversible part and irreversible part

σ = σrev + σirrev. (3.254)

(3.254)

The irreversible part can be calculated using Newtonian fluid theory as

$\mathbf{\sigma}_{\text{irrev}} = -\eta\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right)-\left( {\left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathbf{I},$ (3.255)

(3.255)

So that the complete momentum balance equation can be written as

$\rho\left( {\frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u} = \nabla\left( {\left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}-p} \right) + \nabla \cdot \eta\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right),$ (3.256)

(3.256)

The conservation form can be formulated as

$\frac{\partial\left( {\rho\mathbf{u}} \right)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\rho\mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\nabla \cdot \left( {\mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{J}_{i}} \right)} = \nabla\left( {\left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}-p} \right) + \nabla \cdot \eta\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right)}.$ (3.257)

(3.257)

3.4.3 Thermodynamical consistency

The gradients of the pressure and chemical potentials have the following relation:

$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i} = \nabla p + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i} \otimes \nabla n_{j}} \right).$ (3.258)

(3.258)

Thus the momentum equation formulated in Eq. (3.257) can be reformulated as

$\rho\left( {\frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}} \right) + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u}} = -\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i} + \nabla \cdot \left( {\eta\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right) + \left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathbf{I}} \right),}$ (3.259)

(3.259)

Considering the mass balance Eq. (3.234), we can formulate

$\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} = \left( {\rho\frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t},\mathbf{u}} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\left( {\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t},{|\mathbf{u}|}^{2}} \right) = \left( {\rho\frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t},\mathbf{u}} \right)-\frac{1}{2}\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( \rho\mathbf{u} \right) + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_{i},{|\mathbf{u}|}^{2}}} \right) = \left( {\rho\frac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u} + \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{M_{w,i}\mathbf{J}_{i} \cdot \nabla\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}}} \right) = -\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i},\mathbf{u}} \right) + \left( {\nabla \cdot \left( {\eta\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right) + \left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathbf{I}} \right),\mathbf{u}} \right) = -\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i},\mathbf{u}} \right)-\left( {\eta\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right) + \left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right)\mathbf{I},\nabla\mathbf{u}} \right) = -\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{\left( {n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i},\mathbf{u}} \right)-\left( {\eta\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right),\nabla\mathbf{u}} \right)}-\left( {\left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u},\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right) = -\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {n_{i}\nabla\mu_{i},\mathbf{u}} \right)-\frac{1}{2}\left\| {\eta^{1 \slash 2}\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right)} \right\|^{2}-\left\| {\left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)^{1 \slash 2}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right\|^{2}.$ (3.260)

(3.260)

Multiplying both sides of Eq. (3.233) by μi and integrating it over Ω, we obtain

$\left( {\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t},\mu_{i}} \right) + \left( {\nabla \cdot \left( n_{i}\mathbf{u} \right),\mu_{i}} \right) = \left( {\mathbf{J}_{i},\nabla\mu_{i}} \right).$ (3.261)

(3.261)

Applying the formulation of μi, we derive the summation of the first term on the left-hand side:

$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t},\mu_{i}} \right) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t},\mu_{i}^{b}-\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}{\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{j}} \right)}} \right) = \left( {\frac{\partial f_{b}}{\partial t},1} \right)-\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{\left( {\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t},\nabla \cdot \left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{j}} \right)} \right) = \left( {\frac{\partial f_{b}}{\partial t},1} \right)} + \sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{\left( {\nabla\frac{\partial n_{i}}{\partial t},c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{j}} \right) = \left( {\frac{\partial f_{b}}{\partial t},1} \right)} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{M}{\left( {c_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla n_{i},\nabla n_{j}} \right) = \frac{\partial F}{\partial t}}.$ (3.262)

(3.262)

We denote μ = [μ1,…,μM]T, and further define ${\|\nabla\mathbf{\mu}\|}_{M}^{2}≔-\sum_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {\mathbf{J}_{i},\nabla\mu_{i}} \right) = \sum_{i,j = 1}^{M}\left( \mathcal{M}_{\mathit{ij}}\nabla\mu_{i},\nabla\mu_{j} \right).$ Taking the summation of Eq. (3.261) from i = 1 to M as

$\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = -\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}\left( {\nabla \cdot \left( n_{i}\mathbf{u} \right),\mu_{i}} \right)-{\|\nabla\mathbf{\mu}\|}_{M}^{2}.$ (3.263)

(3.263)

Finally, we can obtain that

$\frac{\partial\left( {F + E} \right)}{\partial t} = -{\|\nabla\mathbf{\mu}\|}_{M}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\eta^{1 \slash 2}\left( {\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{T}} \right)\|^{2}-\left\| {\left( {\xi-\frac{2}{3}\eta} \right)^{1 \slash 2}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}} \right\|^{2},$ (3.264)

(3.264)

and it is easy to see that (∂(F+E))/∂t ≤ 0. It can be stated that the sum of the Helmholtz free energy and kinetic energy is dissipated with time.

Chapter four

Recent progress in Darcy’s scale reservoir simulation

Abstract

Reservoir simulation on Darcy’s scale provides an upscale view of the various processes that are involved in engineering applications. This point of view facilitates greatly the description and the simulation on this relatively direct level. Several algorithms and corresponding solvers have been proposed in the petroleum industry to model and calculate phenomena seen at Darcy’s scale, and plenty of software have been developed using these solvers to help process managing and production estimations. In this chapter, we will go over the notations and model equations of finite element methods (FEMs), first, that are well accepted in Darcy’s scale reservoir simulation, and we will show the equivalence between FEMs and finite-difference methods (FDMs).

Keywords

Galerkin finite element methods; discontinuous Galerkin; IMPES; Darcy’s scale; reactive transport

4.1 Introductions on popular finite element methods

4.1.1 Galerkin finite element methods: general statement

We consider a stationary problem in two dimensions:

 − Δp = f, inΩ,

p = 0, onΓ, (4.1)

(4.1)

where Ω is a bounded domain in the plane with boundary Γ, f is a given real-valued piecewise continuous bounded function in Ω, and the Laplacian operator Δ is defined by

$\Delta p = \frac{\partial^{2}p}{\partial x_{1}^{2}} + \frac{\partial^{2}p}{\partial x_{2}^{2}}.$ (4.2)

(4.2)

which is an elastic membrane fixed at its boundary and subject to a transversal load of intensity f.

We define the linear vector space:

$V = \left\{ \mathit{v:v}{is} a{continuous}{function}{on}\Omega,\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{1}}{and}\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{x}}{is}{piecewise}{continuous}{and}{bounded}{on}\Omega,{and} v = 0{on}\Gamma \right\}.$ (4.3)

(4.3)

Let us recall Green’s formula. For a vector-valued function, b = (b1,b2), the divergence theorem reads:

∫Ω∇ ⋅ b = ∫Γb ⋅ ndl (4.4)

(4.4)

Using Green’s formula:

$\int_{\Omega}{\Delta\mathit{vwd}\mathbf{x}} = \int_{\Gamma}{\frac{\partial v}{\partial\mathbf{n}}\mathit{wdl}} - \int_{\Omega}{\nabla v \cdot \nabla\mathit{wd}\mathbf{x}},$ (4.5)

(4.5)

where the normal derivative is expressed by $\frac{\partial v}{\partial\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{1}}n_{1} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{2}}n_{2}.$

We introduce the notation

a(p,v) :  = ∫Ω∇p ⋅ ∇vdx, L(v) :  = (f,v) :  = ∫Ωfvdx. (4.6)

(4.6)

The form a(⋅,⋅) is called a bilinear form on V × V. We also define the functional F : V→ℝ by

$F\left( v \right) = \frac{1}{2}a\left( v,v \right) - L\left( v \right),v \in V.$ (4.7)

(4.7)

The PDE (partial differential equation) can be formulated as the minimization problem

Findp ∈ VsuchthatF(p) ≤ F(v), ∀v ∈ V. (4.8)

(4.8)

Multiplying the PDE by v ∈ V and integrating over Ω, we see that

 − ∫ΩΔpvdx = ∫Ωfvdx. (4.9)

(4.9)

Applying Green’s formula to this equation and using the homogeneous boundary condition lead to

∫Ω∇p ⋅ ∇vdx = ∫Ωfvdx, ∀v ∈ V. (4.10)

(4.10)

Thus we reach the Galerkin variational form

Findp ∈ Vsuchthata(p,v) = L(v), ∀v ∈ V. (4.11)

(4.11)

We now construct the finite element method (FEM) (

${diam}\left( K \right) = {the}{longest}{edge}{of}\overline{K}\mathit{;h} = \max\limits_{K \in K_{h}}{diam}\left( K \right).$ (4.12)

(4.12)

and the finite element space can be defined as

Vh = {v : visacontinuousfunctiononΩ, vislinearoneachtriangleK ∈ Kh, andv = 0onΓ}. (4.13)

(4.13)

Notice that Vh ⊂ V. The FEM for the PDE is formulated as

Findph ∈ Vhsuchthata(ph,v) = L(v), ∀v ∈ Vh. (4.14)

(4.14)

One can check that the abovementioned finite element formulation is equivalent to a discrete minimization problem:

Findph ∈ VhsuchthatF(ph) ≤ F(v), ∀v ∈ Vh. (4.15)

(4.15)

which is also called the Ritz FEM.

Denote the vertices (nodes) of the triangles in Kh by x1, x2, …, xN. The basis functions φi in Vh, i = 1, 2, …, N are defined by

φi(xj) = 1ifi = j, φi(xj) = 0ifi ≠ j. (4.16)

(4.16)

The support of φi, that is, the set of x where φi(x) ≠ 0, consists of the triangles with the common node xi, and the function φi is also called a hat or chapeau function.

Let N be the number of interior vertices in Kh. Any function v ∈ Vh has the unique representation:

$v\left( \mathbf{x} \right) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{v_{i}\varphi_{i}\left( \mathbf{x} \right)},\mathbf{x} \in \Omega,$ (4.17)

(4.17)

where vi = v(xi). Due to the boundary condition, we exclude the vertices on the boundary of Ω.

The Galerkin formulation can be written in matrix form Ap = f, where the stiffness matrix A and vectors p and f are given by

A = (aij), p = (pj), f = (fj), (4.18)

(4.18)

and it can be checked that the stiffness matrix A is symmetric positive definite. In particular, it is nonsingular. Consequently, the FEM has a unique solution. Also, notice that A is sparse from the construction of the basis functions. In practical computations the entries aij in A are obtained by summing the contributions from different triangles K ∈ Kh:

$a_{\mathit{ij}} = a\left( \varphi_{i},\varphi_{j} \right) = \sum\limits_{K \in K_{h}}{a^{K}\left( \varphi_{i},\varphi_{j} \right)} = \sum\limits_{K \in K_{h}}a_{\mathit{ij}}^{K},$ (4.19)

(4.19)

where aijK :  = aK(φi,φj) :  = ∫K∇φi ⋅ ∇φjdx. Using the definition of the basis functions, we see that aijK = 0 unless nodes xi and xj are both vertices of K.

For single-phase flow in porous media the problem model can be written as

$\begin{matrix} {- \nabla \cdot K\nabla p} & {= q{in}\Omega,} \\ p & {= p_{b}{on}\Gamma_{D},} \\ {- K\nabla p \cdot \mathbf{n}} & {= u_{b}{on}{\Gamma}_{N}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.20)

(4.20)

The weak form reads: to seek p ∈ H0, ΓD(Ω) + E(pb) such that (with pb essential boundary condition (BC) and ub natural BC):

(K∇p,∇v) + ⟨ub, v⟩ΓN = (q,v), ∀v ∈ H0, ΓD(Ω). (4.21)

(4.21)

The Galerkin FEMs reads: to seek ph ∈ Vh + E(pb) such that

(K∇ph,∇v) + ⟨ub, v⟩ΓN = (q,v), ∀v ∈ Vh(Ω). (4.22)

(4.22)

4.1.2 Abstract minimization and variational problems

We consider two problems:

  1. 1. Abstract minimization formulation:

    Findp ∈ VsuchthatF(p) ≤ F(v), ∀v ∈ V, (4.23)

    (4.23)

  2. 2. Abstract variational formulation:

    Findp ∈ Vsuchthata(p,v) = L(v), ∀v ∈ V. (4.24)

    (4.24)


    To analyze these two problems, we first assume the following four properties:

    • • a(⋅,⋅) is symmetric, if a(u,v) = a(v,u), ∀u, v ∈ V.
    • • a(⋅,⋅) is continuous or bounded in the norm ∥ ⋅ ∥V, if there is a constant a *  > 0 such that |a(u,v)| ≤ a*∥u∥V∥v∥V, ∀u, v ∈ V.
    • • a(⋅,⋅) is V-elliptic or coercive, if there exists a constant a *  > 0 such that |a(v,v)| ≥ a*∥v∥V2, ∀v ∈ V.
    • • L is bounded in the norm ||⋅||V:|L(v)|≤L̃||v||V,∀v∈V.

Riesz representation theorem: Let H be a Hilbert space with the scalar product (⋅, ⋅ )H, then for any continuous linear functional L on H, there is a unique u ∈ H such that L(v) = (u, v)H.

Lax–Milgram theorem: Under assumptions of symmetry, boundedness, and V-ellipticity of a(⋅,⋅), and boundedness of L(⋅), the variational problem has a unique solution p ∈ V that satisfies the bound ||p||V≤(L̃/a*).

Proof of Lax–Milgram theorem: Since the bilinear form a is symmetric and V-elliptic, it induces a scalar product in V: [u,v] = a(u,v), u, v ∈ V. By V-ellipticity and boundedness of a(⋅,⋅), we see that

a*∥v∥V2 ≤ [v,v] ≤ a*∥v∥V2, ∀v ∈ V. (4.25)

(4.25)

That is, the norm induced by [⋅,⋅] is equivalent to ∥ ⋅ ∥V. To this new norm, L is still a continuous linear functional. Thus according to the Riesz representation theorem, there is a unique p ∈ V such that [p,v] = L(v), ∀v ∈ V, which show p is the solution.

To show stability, we take v = p in the finite element (FE) formulation and use V-ellipticity of a and boundedness of L to see that

a*||p||V2≤a(p,p)=L(p)≤L̃||p||V, (4.26)

(4.26)

which yields ∥p∥V ≤ (L̃/a*).

Under the four abovementioned assumptions, it can be shown that the minimization problem and the variational problem are equivalent. One can check that the variational problem still possesses a unique solution even without the symmetry assumption. In this case, however, there is no corresponding minimization problem.

Suppose that Vh is a finite element (finite-dimensional) subspace of V. The discrete counterpart of the abstract minimization problem is

Findph ∈ VhsuchthatF(ph) ≤ F(v), ∀v ∈ Vh, (4.27)

(4.27)

The discrete counterpart of the abstract variational problem is

Findph ∈ VhsuchthatF(ph) ≤ F(v), ∀v ∈ Vh, (4.28)

(4.28)

The previous Lax–Milgram theorem remains valid for discrete problems under the four assumptions. Moreover, the solution ph ∈ Vh satisfies ||ph||V≤L̃/a*.

Cea’s lemma (error estimate): Under the four assumptions mentioned earlier, if p and ph are the respective solutions to the abstract variational problem and its discrete counterpart, then

$\| p - p_{h}\|_{V} \leq \frac{a^{*}}{a_{*}}\| p - v\|_{V},\forall v \in V_{h}.$ (4.29)

(4.29)

Proof of Cea’s lemma: Subtracting the abstract variational problem by its discrete counterpart, we see that

a(p−ph,w) = 0, ∀w ∈ Vh. (4.30)

(4.30)

Using boundedness and V-ellipticity of a, for any v ∈ Vh, it follows that

a*∥p − ph∥V2 ≤ a(p−ph,p−ph) = a(p−ph,p−v) ≤ a*∥p − ph∥V∥p − v∥V, (4.31)

(4.31)

which implies our result.

4.1.3 Galerkin finite element methods: settings and notations

The Riemann integral, proposed by Bernhard Riemann (1826–66), is a broadly successful attempt to provide such a foundation. Riemann’s definition starts with the construction of a sequence of easily calculated areas that converge to the integral of a given function. This definition is successful in the sense that it gives the expected answer for many already solved problems and gives useful results for many other problems. However, Riemann integration does not interact well with taking limits of sequences of functions, making such limiting processes difficult to analyze. This is important, for instance, in the study of Fourier series, Fourier transforms, and other topics.

The Lebesgue integral is more useful in describing how and when it is possible to take limits under the integral sign (via the powerful monotone convergence theorem and dominated convergence theorem). While the Riemann integral considers the area under a curve as made out of vertical rectangles, the Lebesgue definition considers horizontal slabs that are not necessarily just rectangles, and so it is more flexible. For example, the Dirichlet function, which is 0 where its argument is irrational and 1 otherwise, has a Lebesgue integral (of zero value) but does not have a Riemann integral. (Recall the intuition that when picking a real number uniformly at random from the unit interval, the probability of picking a rational number should be zero.)

For a real-valued function v on Ω, we use the notation ∫Ωv(x)dx to denote the integral of f in the sense of Lebesgue. For 1 ≤ q < ∞, we define the norm

∥v∥Lq(Ω) :  = (∫Ω|v(x)|qdx)1/q. (4.32)

(4.32)

For q = ∞, we set

∥v∥L∞(Ω) :  = esssup{|v(x)|:x ∈ Ω}, (4.33)

(4.33)

where esssup denotes the essential supremum.

For 1 ≤ q ≤ ∞, we define the Lebesgue spaces

Lq(Ω) :  = {v : visdefinedonΩand∥v∥Lq(Ω) < ∞}. (4.34)

(4.34)

For q = 2, for example, L2(Ω) consists of all square-integrable functions on Ω (in the sense of Lebesgue). A linear space V endowed with a norm ∥ ⋅ ∥ is called a normed linear space. V is termed complete if every Cauchy sequence {vi} in V has a limit v that is an element of V. The Cauchy sequence {vi} means that ∥vi−vj∥→0 as i, j→∞, and completeness says that ∥vi−v∥→0 as i→∞.

A linear space V, together with an inner product (⋅,⋅) defined on it, is called an inner product space and is represented by (V,(⋅,⋅)). With the inner product (⋅,⋅), there is an associated norm defined on V: $\| v\|: = \sqrt{\left( v,v \right)},v \in V.$ Hence an inner product space can be always made to be a normed linear space. A normed linear space (V,∥⋅∥) is called a Banach space, if it is complete with respect to the norm ∥ ⋅ ∥. For 1 ≤ q ≤ ∞ the space Lq(Ω) is a Banach space. An inner product space (V,∥⋅∥) is called a Hilbert space, if it is complete with respect to the norm $\| v\|: = \sqrt{\left( v,v \right)}.$

We introduce the multiindex partial derivative notation:

$D^{\alpha}v = \frac{\partial^{|\alpha|}v}{\partial x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\partial x_{2}^{\alpha_{2}}\cdots\partial x_{d}^{\alpha_{d}}},$ (4.35)

(4.35)

where α = (α1,α2,…,αd) is a multiindex (called a d-tuple), with α1, α2, …, αd nonnegative integers, and |α| = α1 + α2 + ⋯ + αd is the length of α. In calculus, derivatives of a function are defined pointwise. The variational formulation in the FEM is given globally, that is, in terms of integrals on Ω. Hence it is natural to introduce a global definition of derivative more suitable to the Lebesgue spaces.

For Ω ⊂ ℝd, we indicate by 𝒟(Ω) or C0∞(Ω) the subset of C∞(Ω) (i.e., infinitely differentiable) functions that have compact (i.e., bounded and closed) support in Ω. In order to introduce weak derivatives, we define

Lloc1(Ω) :  = {v : v ∈ L1(K)foranycompactKinsideΩ}. (4.36)

(4.36)

We note that C0(Ω) ⊂ Lloc1(Ω) and functions in Lloc1(Ω) can behave arbitrarily badly near the boundary. A function v ∈ Lloc1(Ω) is said to have a weak (generalized) derivative, Dwαv: = u, if there is u ∈ Lloc1(Ω) such that

∫Ωu(x)φ(x)dx = ( − 1)|α|∫Ωv(x)Dαφ(x)dx, ∀φ ∈ 𝒟(Ω). (4.37)

(4.37)

For any multiindex α, if v ∈ C|α|(Ω), the weak derivative Dwαv exists and equals Dαv. Consequently, we will ignore the difference in the definition of Dwα and Dα. Namely, if classical derivatives do not exist, the differentiation symbol Dα will refer to weak derivatives. For r ∈ ℕ and v ∈ Lloc1(Ω), we define the Sobolev norm:

$\| v\|_{W^{r,q}(\Omega)}: = \left( {\sum\limits_{|\alpha| \leq r}{\| D^{\alpha}v\|_{L^{q}(\Omega)}^{q}}} \right)^{1/q},$ (4.38)

(4.38)

if 1 ≤ q < ∞. For q = ∞, we define

$\| v\|_{W^{r,\infty}(\Omega)}: = \max\limits_{|\alpha| \leq r}\| D^{\alpha}v\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}.$ (4.39)

(4.39)

The Sobolev spaces are defined by

Wr, q(Ω) :  = {v ∈ Lloc1(Ω) : ∥v∥Wr, q(Ω) < ∞}, 1 ≤ q ≤ ∞. (4.40)

(4.40)

One can check that ∥ ⋅ ∥Wr, q(Ω) is indeed a norm; moreover, the Sobolev space Wr, q(Ω) is a Banach space. We denote by W0r, q(Ω) the completion of 𝒟(Ω) with respect to the norm ∥ ⋅ ∥Wr, q(Ω). Furthermore, for q = 2, we will utilize the symbols

Hr(Ω) :  = Wr, 2(Ω), H0r(Ω) :  = W0r, 2(Ω), r = 1, 2, ⋯. (4.41)

(4.41)

4.1.4 Mixed finite element methods

In numerical analysis the mixed FEM (MFEM), also known as the hybrid FEM, is a type of FEM in which extra independent variables are introduced as unknown variables during the discretization of a PDE problem. The extra independent variables are constrained by using the Lagrange multipliers. To be distinguished from the MFEM, usual FEMs that do not introduce such extra independent variables are also called irreducible FEMs. The MFEM is efficient for some problems that would be numerically ill-posed if discretized by using the irreducible FEM; one example of such problems is to compute the stress and strain fields in an almost incompressible elastic body (locking effects in the Galerkin FEM).

The reason for using the mixed method is, among others, that in some applications a vector variable (e.g., a fluid velocity) is the primary variable in which one is interested. This is particularly true for flow problems. Then, the mixed method is developed to approximate both the vector variable and a scalar variable (e.g., a pressure) simultaneously and to give a high-order approximation of both variables. Instead of a single finite element space used in the standard FEM, the MFEM employs two different spaces, which suggests the name mixed. For flow problems, another obvious advantage of the MFEM is the mass (or volume) that is conserved locally in each element. In other words, it is locally conservative.

We need one approximation space for the scalar variable (e.g., pressure) and another for the vector variable (e.g., the Darcy velocity). These two spaces must satisfy an inf–sup condition for the mixed method to be stable.

We consider a stationary problem for the unknown p:

$\begin{matrix} {- \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{K}\nabla p \right)} & {= f,{in}\Omega,} \\ p & {= p_{b}{on}\Gamma = \partial\Omega,} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.42)

(4.42)

where Ω ⊂ ℝd (d = 2 or 3) is a bounded 2D or 3D domain with boundary Γ, and f ∈ L2(Ω) is a given function. The mixed variational form reads: Find u ∈ V = H(div,Ω) and p ∈ W = L2(Ω) such that

$\begin{matrix} {\left( \mathbf{K}^{- 1}\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \right) - \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},p \right)} & {= - \int_{\Gamma}{p_{b}\mathbf{v} \cdot \nu}\mathit{ds},\forall\mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{V},} \\ \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u},w \right) & {= \left( f,w \right),\forall w \in W.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.43)

(4.43)

Conductivity K is assumed to be bounded, symmetric, and uniformly positive definite in x: ∀x ∈ Ω, ∀η ∈ ℝd ∖ 0,

$0 < a_{*} \leq {|\eta|}^{- 2}\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{d}{K_{\mathit{ij}}\left( \mathbf{x} \right)\eta_{i}\eta_{j}} \leq a^{*} < \infty.$ (4.44)

(4.44)

There is C1 > 0 such that the inf–sup condition holds

$\underset{0 \neq \mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{V}}{\mathit{\sup}}\frac{|\left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},w \right)|}{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\mathbf{V}}} \geq C_{1}\| w\|,\forall w \in W.$ (4.45)

(4.45)

Because of the property on K (bounded and spd) and the inf–sup condition, the mixed variational form has a unique solution u ∈ V and p ∈ W.

Let Vh ⊂ V and Wh ⊂ W be certain finite-dimensional subspaces. The discrete version of the previous “mixed variational form” is: Find uh ∈ Vh and ph ∈ Wh such that

$\begin{matrix} {\left( \mathbf{K}^{- 1}\mathbf{u}_{h},\mathbf{v} \right) - \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},p_{h} \right)} & {= - \int_{\Gamma}{p_{b}\mathbf{v} \cdot \nu}\mathit{ds},\forall\mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{V}_{h},} \\ \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}_{h},w \right) & {= \left( f,w \right),\forall w \in W_{h}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.46)

(4.46)

For this problem to have a unique solution, it is natural to impose a discrete inf–sup condition:

$\underset{0 \neq \mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{V}_{h}}{\mathit{\sup}}\frac{|\left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},w \right)|}{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\mathbf{V}}} \geq C_{2}\| w\|_{W},\forall w \in W_{h},$ (4.47)

(4.47)

where C2 > 0 is a constant independent of h.

The condition next is for the solvability of MFEM:

$\sup\limits_{0 \neq \mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{V}_{h}}\frac{|\left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},w \right)|}{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\mathbf{V}}} \geq C_{2}\| w\|_{W},\forall w \in W_{h}.$ (4.48)

(4.48)

The condition can be rewritten as

$\inf\limits_{0 \neq w \in W_{h}}\sup\limits_{0 \neq \mathbf{v} \in \mathbf{V}_{h}}\frac{|\left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},w \right)|}{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\mathbf{V}}\| w\|_{W}} \geq C_{2} > 0.$ (4.49)

(4.49)

It is the (discrete) stability condition, also known as the discrete inf–sup condition. It is also called the Babuska–Brezzi condition or sometimes the Ladyshenskaja–Babuska–Brezzi condition.

For Ω ⊂ ℝ2, let 𝒦h be a partition of Ω into triangles such that adjacent elements completely share their common edge. For a triangle K ∈ 𝒦h, let

Pr(K) = {v : visapolynomialofdegreeatmostronK}, (4.50)

(4.50)

where r ≥ 0 is an integer. Mixed finite element spaces Vh × Wh are defined locally on each element K ∈ 𝒦h, so let

Vh(K) = Vh|K (4.51)

(4.51)

(the restriction of Vh to K) and

Wh(K) = Wh|K. (4.52)

(4.52)

Raviart-Thomas (RT) spaces on triangles are the first mixed finite element spaces introduced by

Vh(K) = (Pr(K))2 ⊕ ((x1,x2)Pr(K)), Wh(K) = Pr(K), (4.53)

(4.53)

where the notation ⊕ indicates a direct sum. For r = 0, we observe that Vh(K) has the form

Vh(K) = {v : v = (bKx1+aK,bKx2+cK), aK, bK, cK ∈ ℝ}, (4.54)

(4.54)

and its dimension is three. In the case r = 0, as the degrees of freedom (DOF) to describe the functions in Vh, we use the values of normal components of the functions at the midpoints of edges in 𝒦h, and the DOF for Wh can be the averages of functions over K. In general, for r ≥ 0, the dimensions of Vh(K) and Wh(K) are

$\dim\left( \mathbf{V}_{h}\left( K \right) \right) = \left( r + 1 \right)\left( r + 3 \right),\dim\left( W_{h}\left( K \right) \right) = \frac{\left( r + 1 \right)\left( r + 2 \right)}{2}.$ (4.55)

(4.55)

The DOF for the space Vh(K), with r ≥ 0, are given by

(v ⋅ ν, w)e, ∀w ∈ Pr(e), e ∈ ∂K, (4.56)

(4.56)

(v, w)K, ∀w ∈ (Pr − 1(K))2. (4.57)

(4.57)

This is indeed a legitimate choice; that is, a function in Vh(K) is uniquely determined by these DOF. It is a square system and uniqueness implies existence.

We now consider the case where Ω is a rectangular domain and 𝒦h is a partition of Ω into rectangles such that the horizontal and vertical edges of rectangles are parallel to the x1- and x2-coordinate axes, respectively, and adjacent elements completely share their common edge. Define

$Q_{l,r}\left( K \right): = \left\{ {\mathit{v:v}\left( \mathbf{x} \right) = \sum\limits_{i = 0}^{l}{\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{r}{v_{\mathit{ij}}x_{1}^{i}x_{2}^{j}}},\mathbf{x} = \left( x_{1},x_{2} \right) \in K,v_{\mathit{ij}} \in \mathbb{R}} \right\}.$ (4.58)

(4.58)

That is, Ql, r(K) is the space of polynomials of degree at most l in x1 and r in x2, l,r ≥ 0.

The RT spaces on rectangles are an extension of the RT spaces on triangles to rectangles (

$\begin{matrix} {\mathbf{V}_{h}(K) = Q_{r + 1,r}(K) \times Q_{r,r + 1}(K),} \\ {W_{h}\left( K \right) = Q_{r,r}\left( K \right).} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.59)

(4.59)

In the case r = 0, Vh(K) takes the form:

Vh(K) = {v : v = (aK1+aK2x1,aK3+aK4x2), aKi ∈ ℝ, i = 1, 2, 3, 4}. (4.60)

(4.60)

and its dimension is four. The DOF for Vh(K) are the values of normal components of functions at the midpoint on each edge in 𝒦h. For a general r ≥ 0 the dimensions of Vh(K) and Wh(K) are

$\begin{array}{l} {\dim(\mathbf{V}_{h}(K)) = 2(r + 1)(r + 2),} \\ {\dim(W_{h}(K)) = {(r + 1)}^{2}.} \\ \end{array}$ (4.61)

(4.61)

The DOF for Vh(K) are given by

$\begin{matrix} {{(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nu,w)}_{e},\forall w \in P_{r}(e),e \in \partial K,} \\ {{(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})}_{K},\forall\mathbf{w} \in Q_{r - 1,r}(K) \times Q_{r,r - 1}(K).} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.62)

(4.62)

The BDM (or Brezzi–Douglas–Marini) spaces (Brezzi et al., 1985) on rectangles differ considerably from the RT spaces on rectangles: The vector elements are based on augmenting the space of vector polynomials of total degree r by exactly two additional vectors in place of augmenting the space of vector tensor–products of polynomials of degree r by 2r + 2 polynomials of higher degree. Besides, a lower dimensional space for the scalar variable is used. The BDM spaces, for any r ≥ 1 are given by

$\begin{matrix} {\mathbf{V}_{h}(K) = {(P_{r}(K))}^{2} \oplus {span}\left\{ \mathbf{c}\mathbf{u}\mathbf{r}\mathbf{l}(x_{1}^{r + 1}x_{2}),\mathbf{c}\mathbf{u}\mathbf{r}\mathbf{l}(x_{1}x_{2}^{r + 1}) \right\},} \\ {W_{h}(K) = P_{r - 1}(K).} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.63)

(4.63)

In the case r = 1, Vh(K) can be represented by

$\begin{matrix} \left\{ \mathbf{v}:\mathbf{v} = (v_{1},v_{2}),v_{1} = (a_{K}^{1} + a_{K}^{2}x_{1} + a_{K}^{3}x_{2} - a_{K}^{4}x_{1}^{2} - 2a_{K}^{5}x_{1}x_{2}), \right. \\ \left. v_{2} = (a_{K}^{6} + a_{K}^{7}x_{1} + a_{K}^{8}x_{2} + 2a_{K}^{4}x_{1}x_{2} + a_{K}^{5}x_{2}^{2}), \right\} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.64)

(4.64)

and its dimension is eight. The DOF for Vh(K) are the values of normal components of functions at the two quadratic Gauss points on each edge in 𝒦h. For any r ≥ 1, the dimensions of Vh(K) and Wh(K) are

$\begin{matrix} {\dim(\mathbf{V}_{h}(K)) = (r + 1)(r + 2) + 2,} \\ {\dim(W_{h}(K)) = \frac{r(r + 1)}{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.65)

(4.65)

The DOF for Vh(K) are

$\begin{matrix} {{(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nu,w)}_{e},\forall w \in P_{r}(e),e \in \partial K,} \\ {{(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})}_{K},\forall\mathbf{w} \in {(P_{r - 2}(K))}^{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.66)

(4.66)

The MFEM can be recast in matrix form:

$\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{B}^{T} & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{u} \\ \mathbf{p} \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{g} \\ {- \mathbf{f}} \\ \end{pmatrix}.$ (4.67)

(4.67)

The overall matrix

$M = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{B}^{T} & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ (4.68)

(4.68)

is nonsingular under the inf–sup condition, but it is not positive definite. This limits application of many iterative algorithms to the resultant algebraic equations.

The Uzawa algorithm (

$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}^{k} = \mathbf{g} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{p}^{k - 1},} \\ {\mathbf{p}^{k} = \mathbf{p}^{k - 1} + \alpha(\mathbf{B}^{T}\mathbf{u}^{k} + \mathbf{f}),} \\ \end{array}$ (4.69)

(4.69)

where α is a given real number. To see convergence of The Uzawa algorithm, we define the residual:

ek :  =  − BTuk − f. (4.70)

(4.70)

We note that

BTA − 1Bp = BTA − 1g + f. (4.71)

(4.71)

Using the abovementioned equation and the algorithm, we see that

ek =  − BTA − 1(g−Bpk − 1) − f =  − BTA − 1B(p−pk − 1). (4.72)

(4.72)

So

pk − pk − 1 =  − αek = αBTA − 1B(p−pk − 1). (4.73)

(4.73)

4.1.5 Mixed–hybrid finite element methods

The usual mixed formulation requires the solution of a linear system in the form of a saddle point problem, which can be expensive to solve. An alternate approach is proposed then involving the hybrid (or the Lagrange multiplier) form of the equations. In this method, one eliminates the pressure and velocity unknowns in terms of the Lagrange multipliers. There are more overall unknowns: the lowest order RT spaces have one the Lagrange multiplier unknown per edge if d = 2 or per face if d = 3. It is simple to implement and requires the solution of a sparse, positive semidefinite linear system.

For convenience of presentation, we assume pb = 0 in the model problem. That is, we now consider a stationary problem for the unknown p:

$\begin{matrix} {- \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{K}\nabla p \right)} & {= f,{in}\Omega,} \\ p & {= 0{on}\Gamma = \partial\Omega,} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.74)

(4.74)

where Ω ⊂ ℝd (d = 2 or 3) is a bounded 2D or 3D domain with boundary Γ, and f ∈ L2(Ω) is a given function.

We recall

Vh :  = {v ∈ V : v|K ∈ Vh(K)∀K ∈ 𝒦h}. (4.75)

(4.75)

The constraint Vh ⊂ V implies that the normal components of the functions in Vh are continuous across the interior boundaries in 𝒦h. Following

${\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}}_{h}: = \left\{ \mathbf{v} \in \left( {L^{2}\left( \Omega \right)} \right)^{d}:\mathbf{v}|_{K} \in \mathbf{V}_{h}\left( K \right)\forall K \in \mathcal{K}_{h} \right\}.$ (4.76)

(4.76)

We note that Vh ⊂ V and $\mathbf{V}_{h} \subset {\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}}_{h}$, but ${\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}}_{h} ⊄ \mathbf{V}$.

We need to introduce the Lagrange multipliers to enforce the required continuity on ${\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}}_{h}$. In order to do this, we define

$L_{h}: = \{\mu \in L^{2}\left( \bigcup\limits_{e \in \mathcal{E}_{h}}e \right):{\mu|}_{e} \in {\mathbf{V}_{h} \cdot \nu|}_{e}\forall e \in \mathcal{E}_{h}\},$ (4.77)

(4.77)

where ℰh indicates the set of all edges or faces in 𝒦h.

The hybrid form of the mixed method is: Find (uh,ph,λh) $\in {\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}}_{h} \times W_{h} \times L_{h}$ such that

$\begin{matrix} {\left( {\mathbf{u}_{h},\mathbf{v}} \right) - \sum\limits_{K \in \mathcal{K}_{h}}\left( {\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},p_{h}} \right)_{K} - \mathbf{v} \cdot \nu_{K},\lambda_{h\partial K \smallsetminus \Gamma}} \right) = 0,\quad\forall v \in {\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}}_{h},} \\ {\sum\limits_{K \in \mathcal{K}_{h}}\left( {\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}_{h},w} \right)_{K} = \left( {f,w} \right),\quad\forall w \in W_{h},} \\ {\sum\limits_{K \in \mathcal{K}_{h}}\left\langle {\mathbf{u}_{h} \cdot \nu_{K},\mu} \right\rangle_{\partial K \smallsetminus \Gamma} = 0,\quad\forall\mu \in L_{h},} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.78)

(4.78)

where νK denotes the outward unit normal to K. Note that the abovementioned third equation enforces the continuity requirement on uh. In fact, we have uh ∈ Vh. The matrix form could be expressed as

$\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{C} \\ \mathbf{B}^{T} & 0 & 0 \\ \mathbf{C}^{T} & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{u} \\ \mathbf{p} \\ \lambda \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ {- \mathbf{f}} \\ 0 \\ \end{pmatrix},$ (4.79)

(4.79)

where λ is the DOF of λh. The advantage of the system previously is that the matrix A is block diagonal, with each block corresponding to a single element. Hence A is easily inverted at the element level. Taking advantage of the fact that the matrix A is block diagonal (hence A − 1 can be easily obtained), the first equation in the matrix form of the mixed–hybrid FEM (MHFEM) leads to

u =  − A − 1Bp − A − 1Cλ. (4.80)

(4.80)

Substituting it into the second and third equations in the matrix form of the MFHEM, we see that

$\begin{matrix} {\mathbf{B}^{T}\mathbf{A}^{- 1}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{B}^{T}\mathbf{A}^{- 1}\mathbf{C}\lambda = \mathbf{f},} \\ {\mathbf{C}^{T}\mathbf{A}^{- 1}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{C}^{T}\mathbf{A}^{- 1}\mathbf{C}\lambda = \mathbf{f}.} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.81)

(4.81)

We note BTA − 1B is symmetric and positive definite, so the first equation of the algebraic equation (AE) system in Eq. (4.81) yields:

p = (BTA − 1B) − 1f − (BTA − 1B) − 1BTA − 1Cλ. (4.82)

(4.82)

Substituting this equation into the second equation of the AE system in Eq. (4.81) implies the linear system for λ:

(CTA − 1C − (CTA − 1B)(BTA − 1B) − 1(BTA − 1C))λ =  − (CTA − 1B)(BTA − 1B) − 1f. (4.83)

(4.83)

This system for λ is symmetric, positive definite, and sparse. We can solve it for λ (via e.g., an iterative algorithm), recover p, and then recover u.

From another point of view, we note that, after reordering the unknowns within u and within p, the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{B}^{T} & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ becomes a block-diagonal matrix (denoted as D), with each block corresponding to a single element. We thus can invert the matrix D (and thus the 2 × 2 block matrix above) easily at the element level. The unknowns u and p can be solved by the equation system next, if λ is given:

$\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{B}^{T} & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{u} \\ \mathbf{p} \\ \end{pmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{C} \\ 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \lambda \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ {- \mathbf{f}} \\ \end{pmatrix}.$ (4.84)

(4.84)

After local computation, we can obtain the unknowns u and p, if λ is given:

$\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{u} \\ \mathbf{p} \\ \end{pmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{B}^{T} & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}^{- 1}\begin{pmatrix} {\mathbf{C}\lambda} \\ \mathbf{f} \\ \end{pmatrix}.$ (4.85)

(4.85)

It can be noted that inverting the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{B}^{T} & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ involves only local computation at the element level. Substituting this equation into the third equation of the AE system (as listed in Eq. 4.81) implies the linear system for λ.

4.2 Links between finite-difference methods and finite element methods

4.2.1 Model problem

We consider a stationary problem for the unknown p,

$\begin{matrix} {- \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{K}\nabla p \right)} & {= f,{in}\Omega,} \\ p & {= 0{on}\Gamma = \partial\Omega,} \\ \end{matrix}$ (4.86)

(4.86)

where Ω ⊂ ℝd is a bounded one-dimensional (1D), 2D, or 3D domain with boundary Γ, and f ∈ L2(Ω) is a given function. Conductivity K is assumed to be bounded, symmetric, and uniformly positive definite in x: ∀x ∈ Ω, ∀η ∈ ℝd ∖ 0,

$0 < a_{*} \leq {|\eta|}^{- 2}\sum\limits_{i,j = 1}^{d}{K_{\mathit{ij}}\left( \mathbf{x} \right)\eta_{i}\eta_{j}} \leq a^{*} < \infty.$ (4.87)

(4.87)

We assume that Ω is a rectangular domain. Let Th be a partition of Ω into nonoverlapping (open) elements Ei that are intervals (1D), rectangles (2D), or rectangles (3D). Conductivity K is assumed to be a diagonal tensor with cell-wise constant coefficients. For example, if 2D, we have

$\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} K^{\mathit{xx}} & 0 \\ 0 & K^{\mathit{yy}} \\ \end{bmatrix},$ (4.88)

(4.88)
